title: Piecewise & step functions
examples: How do I know which piece of the function to use?
What does it mean for a function to be continuous at a join point?
Can you show an example of a step function in the real world?

explain.say: Today we learn about piecewise functions. These functions use different rules for different inputs. Think of it like having different tools for different jobs. We will learn to define and sketch these functions.
A piecewise function is defined by several smaller functions. Each piece has its own specific domain or input range. We must look at the conditions to know which rule to use for a given x value.

items: Each piece has its own specific domain
Must look at conditions for x value

explain.say: Consider a function defined as x squared if x is less than zero. And it is x plus one if x is greater than or equal to zero. This shows two separate rules working together.

draw.text: f(x) = x² if x < 0; x + 1 if x ≥ 0

explain.say: Next we look at continuity at the joins. For a function to be continuous, the pieces must meet up perfectly. The limit from the left must equal the limit from the right.

items: Left limit must equal right limit

explain.say: Let us check the join point at x equals zero for our example. The left side approaches zero squared, which is zero. The right side approaches zero plus one, which is one. Since zero does not equal one, the function is not continuous there.

faq.q: What is the difference between a piecewise function and a step function?
faq.a: A step function is a specific type of piecewise function. It usually takes on constant values over intervals. It looks like a series of steps on a graph.
asks: What makes a function a step function?

faq.q: If the function is not continuous, what does that mean on a graph?
faq.a: It means there is a break or a jump in the line graph. The graph suddenly jumps from one value to another at that point.
asks: What does a discontinuity look like?
Can a function jump on a graph?

faq.q: How do I test for continuity at a point like x equals two?
faq.a: You must check three things. First, the function must be defined there. Second, the limit must exist. Third, the limit must equal the function value.
asks: What are the three conditions for continuity?
How do I check if a function is continuous?

faq.q: Does the inequality matter when I sketch the graph?
faq.a: Yes, the inequality determines if the point is included. A less than sign means an open circle. Greater than or equal to means a closed circle.
asks: What do open and closed circles mean?
How do I draw the boundaries correctly?

faq.q: Can a function be continuous everywhere?
faq.a: Yes, if the rules defining the pieces connect smoothly. This means the function value matches up at every join point.
asks: Does it have to be smooth?

facts: A piecewise function uses different formulas for different parts of its domain.
For a function to be continuous at a point, the left-hand limit must equal the right-hand limit.
If the function value is defined by 'greater than' only, use an open circle at the boundary.
Step functions are characterized by constant values over specific intervals.

quiz.say: If f(x) = 2x and f(x) = x + 5, and the join is at x=1, what is the value of the left limit?
quiz.why: The left limit uses the first piece, 2x, so 2 times 1 equals 2.

wrong.0: This incorrectly uses the value from the second function for the left side.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses the right side's value for the left side calculation.
wrong.3: This calculates the average of the two function values, which is not the correct mathematical operation.

quiz.say: A function defined by f(x) = 3 if x < 0 and f(x) = x² if x ≥ 0 has a jump discontinuity at x=0. What is the value of the right limit?
quiz.why: The right limit uses the second piece, x squared, so 0 squared equals 0.

wrong.0: This calculates the value of the first piece at x=0, ignoring the rule for the right side.
wrong.1: The limit exists because both sides approach a defined number, even if they are different.
wrong.3: This incorrectly uses the value from the first piece for the right side calculation.

quiz.say: For a function to be continuous at x=a, which statement must be true?

options.show: The right limit must equal f(a).
options.say: The right limit must equal f(a).

options.show: The left limit must equal the right limit.
options.say: The left limit must equal the right limit.

options.show: The left limit must equal the right limit, and both must equal f(a).
options.say: The left limit must equal the right limit, and both must equal f(a).

options.show: The left limit must equal f(a).
options.say: The left limit must equal f(a).

quiz.why: All three values must match perfectly for the graph to have no breaks or jumps.

wrong.0: This ignores the requirement that the left side must also match the function value.
wrong.1: This only checks for the limit existing, but not if the function is actually defined at that point.
wrong.3: This ignores the requirement that the right side must also match the function value.
